metadata.title: Assessment of ChatGPT performance in orbital MRI reporting with multimetric evaluation of transformer based language models

abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT-4, are increasingly used to streamline clinical practice, of which radiology reporting is a prominent aspect. However, their performance in interpreting complex anatomical regions from MRI data remains largely unexplored. This study investigates the capability of ChatGPT-4 to produce clinically reliable reports based on orbital MR images, applying a multimetric, quantitative evaluation framework in 25 patients with orbital lesions. Due to inherent limitations of current version of GPT-4, the model was not fed with MR volumetric data, but key 2D images only. For each case, ChatGPT-4 generated a free-text report, which was then compared to the corresponding ground-truth report authored by a board-certified radiologist. Evaluation included established NLP metrics (BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, BERTScore), clinical content recognition scores (RadGraph F1, CheXbert), and expert human judgment. Among the automated metrics, BERTScore demonstrated the highest language similarity, while RadGraph F1 best captured clinical entity recognition. Clinician assessment revealed moderate agreement with the LLM outputs, with performance decreasing in complex or infiltrative cases. The study highlights both the promise and current limitations of LLMs in radiology, particularly regarding their inability to process volumetric data and maintain spatial consistency. These findings suggest that while LLMs may assist in structured reporting, effective integration into diagnostic imaging workflows will require coupling with advanced vision models capable of full 3D interpretation.

key_findings.claim: BERTScore achieved the highest language similarity between ChatGPT 4o-generated and expert radiologist orbital MRI reports among all evaluated NLP metrics.
key_findings.context: Pilot study of 25 orbital lesion MRI cases; compared against BLEU-4 (0.4140) and ROUGE-L (0.4988)

key_findings.claim: RadGraph F1 outperformed CheXbert similarity in evaluating clinical content completeness of LLM-generated orbital MRI reports.
key_findings.context: RadGraph F1 captures entity relationships; CheXbert is a keyword-based proxy not optimized for orbital imaging

key_findings.claim: ChatGPT 4o performed significantly better on well-circumscribed orbital lesions than on infiltrative lesions across all automated and clinician-assessed metrics.
key_findings.quantitative_result: BERTScore 0.75 vs 0.62; RadGraph F1 0.55 vs 0.42; CheXbert 0.50 vs 0.35; clinical completeness 0.60 vs 0.40; diagnostic accuracy 0.55 vs 0.35; clinical utility 0.58 vs 0.38 (all p < 0.05, Mann-Whitney U)
key_findings.context: 25 cases stratified into well-circumscribed vs infiltrative lesion categories

key_findings.claim: Almost half of the 25 cases assessed by clinicians received a low or very low clinical utility score for the ChatGPT-generated reports.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Clinical utility scored low or very low in approximately 50% of cases; clinical utility = 0.7 × diagnostic accuracy + 0.3 × clinical completeness
key_findings.context: Evaluated by five maxillofacial surgeons; clinical utility scale: very low 0–0.3, low 0.3–0.5, moderate 0.5–0.7, high 0.7–1.0

key_findings.claim: Inter-observer agreement among five maxillofacial surgeons evaluating LLM report quality was substantial for all three clinician-assessed metrics.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Cohen's kappa: clinical completeness κ = 0.83, diagnostic accuracy κ = 0.87, clinical utility κ = 0.84
key_findings.context: Five independent evaluators assessed 25 cases; no formal adjudication required due to high agreement

key_findings.claim: Current ChatGPT architecture cannot natively process volumetric NIfTI or DICOM data, requiring 2D screenshot workarounds for MRI report generation tasks.
key_findings.context: Technical limitation requiring multiplanar screenshots (axial, coronal, sagittal) as proxies for volumetric interpretation

key_findings.claim: BERTScore is superior to BLEU and ROUGE-L for evaluating radiology report quality because it captures semantic equivalence via contextual embeddings rather than exact n-gram matching.
key_findings.context: Particularly relevant for medical terminology where paraphrasing is common (e.g., 'vascular mass' vs 'hemangioma')

llm_extraction.methods_summary: Pilot study comparing ChatGPT 4o-generated radiology reports against board-certified radiologist ground-truth reports for 25 orbital MRI lesions from two Italian academic medical centers (University of Udine and San Paolo Hospital Milan). MRI data were exported as NIfTI files, preprocessed to 256×256 pixels PNG screenshots in three orthogonal planes (axial, coronal, sagittal), normalized, and fed to GPT-4o via standardized prompts. The model used its integrated visual encoder and language module to generate structured radiology reports end-to-end without external segmentation pipelines. Evaluation used five automated NLP metrics (BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, BERTScore, RadGraph F1, CheXbert similarity) and three clinician-assessed metrics (clinical completeness, diagnostic accuracy, clinical utility) scored by five maxillofacial surgeons. Inter-observer agreement was quantified with Cohen's kappa. Performance was stratified by lesion morphology (well-circumscribed vs infiltrative) using Mann-Whitney U tests.
llm_extraction.limitations: Small pilot sample (n=25) limits statistical power and generalizability. GPT-4o cannot process volumetric data natively; 2D screenshot workaround loses 3D spatial information. Radiology reports used as ground-truth may themselves contain stylistic variability or inconsistencies, introducing confounding bias. LLM requires explicit declaration of radiological laterality convention (screen-right ≠ patient-right), which may not be standard in real-world deployment. CheXbert was developed for chest X-ray and is not optimized for orbital imaging, making it an imprecise proxy metric. Study evaluates only one commercial LLM (ChatGPT 4o) without comparison to specialized radiology AI platforms (Aidoc, Viz.ai, Gleamer, Arterys). LLM showed substantially poorer performance on infiltrative lesions with poorly defined margins. Clinician evaluation was performed by maxillofacial surgeons rather than radiologists, which may affect domain-specific scoring. No blinding of evaluators to report source (AI vs human) is described.

methodology_details.approach: Structured comparison of ChatGPT 4o-generated orbital MRI reports versus board-certified radiologist reports using multimetric NLP and clinician evaluation framework
datasets: 25 orbital MRI lesion cases from University of Udine Academic Hospital and San Paolo Hospital Milan (IRB_45_2020)
metrics: Clinical utility (composite: 0.7 × diagnostic accuracy + 0.3 × clinical completeness)
methodology_details.reproducibility_notes: Standardized prompt structure used across all cases; images normalized to uniform voxel size 1×1×1 mm and 256×256 pixel PNG format; metrics computed in ChatGPT and verified in MATLAB; all data reported in supplementary materials; ethical approval and informed consent obtained

domain_specific_fields.benchmark: Multimetric evaluation of ChatGPT 4o on orbital MRI radiology report generation, pilot study of 25 cases
domain_specific_fields.model_architecture: GPT-4o (transformer-based multimodal LLM with integrated visual encoder; 2D image understanding via built-in ViT-style tokenization; no external CNN or volumetric pipeline)
domain_specific_fields.dataset: 25 orbital MRI lesions (T1 or T2 weighted, with or without contrast enhancement) from two Northern Italian academic maxillofacial surgery centers
